title: A novel stomata-opening compound that inhibits the abscisic acid pathway
content: Stomata are small pores on the surface of leaves that regulate the uptake of CO₂, a substrate for photosynthesis, and control water transport through transpiration. Stomata are surrounded by guard cells, which swell to open the stomata or shrink to close them. Stomatal opening and closure are regulated by environmental cues: stomata generally open when exposed to light and low CO2 levels but close in response to darkness, high CO2 levels, water deficit, and pathogen invasion (Hou et al. 2024). Stomatal movement is regulated by complex molecular signaling mechanisms; for instance, the plasma membrane (PM) H+-ATPase is an enzyme that pumps protons from the intracellular space to the extracellular space, creating a driving force for stomatal opening. Blue light induces the phosphorylation of a penultimate residue, Thr948 (pen-Thr, numbering according to Arabidopsis thaliana H+-ATPase 1), a modification required for its activation (Kinoshita and Shimazaki 1999). Activation of PM H+-ATPase induces proton extrusion, leading to hyperpolarization of the guard cell membrane. This hyperpolarization activates voltage-dependent inward-rectifying K+ channels in the guard cell membrane, facilitating K+ uptake. The resulting increase in osmotic pressure drives water influx, causing the flanking guard cells to swell. Their expansion and separation from each other ultimately cause the stomata to open (Inoue and Kinoshita 2017). In contrast, abscisic acid (ABA) promotes stomatal closure and regulates water-use efficiency. ABA is perceived by PYRABACTIN RESISTANCE 1/PYR1-LIKE/REGULATORY COMPONENT OF ABA RECEPTOR (PYR/PYL/RCAR) receptors, which interact with and inactivate PP2C phosphatases, thereby relieving their inhibition on subclass III SNF1-related protein kinases (SnRK2s). In guard cells, OPEN STOMATA 1/SnRK2.6 phosphorylate substrates, including slow anion channel 1 (SLAC1), lead to depolarization of the guard cell membrane. It is also important to note that ABA can trigger an increase in cytosolic calcium levels, which represents another signaling pathway that can lead to SLAC1 activation. Consequently, outward-rectifying K+ channels are activated, and the efflux of K+ from guard cells ensues, resulting in stomatal closure (Hsu et al. 2021). Furthermore, ABA signaling also suppresses light-dependent stomatal opening (Hayashi et al. 2011), but the underlying molecular mechanism remains unclear, in part due to the substantial genetic redundancy among genes regulating stomatal movement. This redundancy complicates the functional analysis of individual components.
